title: Other people's opinions
hookLine: what others think is on their side of the line; how we treat them is on ours (Enchiridion 1)

cards: You post a photo and check it again, and again, before the hour is up. You say something in a meeting and spend the evening replaying the face your colleague made.
A relative says at dinner, so you're still doing that job? And it rattles around your head for a week. Other people's opinions of you: you try hard to steer them, and have very little grip on them.
Epictetus put them on his list, and his line runs right through the middle of the dinner table.

teach.b: Go back to the Handbook's first lines. On the not-up-to-us list, right after the body and property, Epictetus puts reputation: what other people think and say of us.
On the up-to-us list, first of all, he puts our own opinions and judgments. That's the line. Their opinion of me: their side.
My opinion, and what I do next: my side. Marcus Aurelius noticed how odd this is.
He wonders, in the Meditations, how each of us loves ourselves more than anyone else, and yet cares more about what others think of us than what we think of ourselves.
Epictetus adds a sharp practical point elsewhere in the Handbook.

teach.h: THEY DIDN'T KNOW MY OTHER FAULTS.
teach.b: If someone speaks badly of you, don't defend yourself; answer, in paraphrase, that they clearly didn't know your other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. It's a joke, and it's also freedom.
The line has two sides, and the second matters as much as the first. Their opinion is theirs to think.

teach.h: HOW I TREAT THEM IS MINE.
teach.b: But how you treat them is yours. Letting go of what someone thinks is not the same as not caring about them.

You can let your relative's comment stay theirs, and still pass the potatoes warmly, still ask how their knee is. It's easier, in fact: when you stop trying to win their verdict, your hands are free to be kind.
And if the criticism has something true in it, that's yours to use, quietly, without needing them to see you do it.

how: People who practice Stoicism often treat reputation as not up to them, following Enchiridion 1, and turn their attention to their own judgments and how they treat others.

o: a Greek prayer book read before meals
Epictetus's handbook of what's up to us
a Roman law code on property

games.q: which side of the line — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says to defend yourself when someone speaks badly of you
he jokes: say they didn't know your other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too.
Marcus noticed we love ourselves most, yet care more what others think of us
he wonders at it in the Meditations.
letting an opinion stay theirs means you stop caring about them
their opinion is theirs; how you treat them is still yours. letting go frees your hands to be kind.

games.q: someone tells you a coworker has been criticizing you behind your back. what does Epictetus suggest?
o: say they clearly didn't know your other faults.
find the coworker and set the record straight.
criticize them back, so it's even.
games.why: don't defend yourself; answer that they didn't know your other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. a joke, and a freedom.

practice: Bring to mind one opinion someone holds of you that bothers you, a comment, a look, a silence, and notice where you feel it in your body. On an out-breath, picture handing it back across the table: that's yours to think.
Then ask if anything in it is true and useful; keep that small piece, and set the rest down.

wordCard.voice: Enchiridion. Epictetus's Handbook, where he puts their opinion of you on their side of the line, and how you treat them on yours. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: opinion, reputation, what people think of you. In Enchiridion 1, the plural, δόξαι, names reputation.

carryVoice: Your line: theirs to think. How you treat them stays yours. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Enchiridion 1 (reputation among things not up to us)
